query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys exposed to high-temperature oxidizing environments, the interplay between an engineered lamellar/nanocrystalline microstructure and lattice distortion governs oxidation resistance and material integrity. Specifically, high lattice distortion elevates vacancy formation energies, suppressing the outward diffusion of key reactive elements (such as Al) that form protective oxides. Concurrently, the refined microstructure promotes the rapid establishment of a layered oxide scale—an inner, slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 layer followed by outer Mn/Cr-rich oxides—that together hinder both oxygen ingress and further cation diffusion, thereby reducing oxidation kinetics and mitigating scale spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal-element alloy (e.g., a CoCrFeNiMn or FeNiCuAl-based alloy) in a homogeneous and super-saturated solid solution state, with the potential for producing a lamellar eutectic or nanocrystalline microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to isothermal oxidation at high temperatures (e.g., 1200°C in air) for extended durations while comparing samples processed to have either (i) a highly refined, high lattice distortion microstructure or (ii) a coarser microstructure with lower lattice distortion.
generation.conditions: Controlled oxidation tests in ambient air at 900–1200°C for durations up to 500 hours, ensuring similar oxygen partial pressures and minimal variations in bulk composition apart from the microstructural refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: The lamellar eutectic or ultrafine-grain structure—which provides both fast diffusion paths for initial protective oxide formation and sites for enhanced lattice distortion—and the resultant diffusion-hampering effect on key elements like Al.
generation.mechanism: High lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for vacancy formation, thereby retarding the outward diffusion of reactive elements such as Al. This suppression slows the growth of the oxide scale according to diffusion-controlled (parabolic) kinetics. At the same time, the tailored microstructure accelerates the early formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer and subsequent layered oxide formation (with Mn/Cr-rich regions), which together serve as an effective barrier to further oxidation and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys exhibiting higher lattice distortion and a refined lamellar microstructure will show significantly lower oxidation rate constants (i.e., reduced mass gain over time), thinner and more adherent oxide scales, and improved retention of mechanical integrity compared to baseline alloys with coarser, less distorted structures.
generation.baseline: A reference multiprincipal-element alloy with similar overall composition but with a conventional, coarser microstructure and lower lattice distortion (e.g., a typical MCrAlY alloy), which is expected to form thicker, less adherent oxide layers and exhibit faster oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for multiprincipal-element alloys where protective oxides (such as Al2O3) are the primary oxidation barrier and where the composition does not lead to the formation of volatile oxides (e.g., excessive Ti-induced oxides). Its applicability may be limited in systems where other elements dominate oxidation behavior or where processing cannot impart significant lattice distortion.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on the diffusion suppression mechanism observed in the MPEA with lattice distortion (PMC13067856::web::000::abstract) and the layered oxide formation insights from the speciated oxidation study (PMC11169556::web::000::abstract). The novel aspect is the combined emphasis on how microstructural refinement (lamellar/nanocrystalline) and lattice distortion synergistically control oxidation kinetics and scale adhesion in MPEAs. Uncertainties remain in quantitatively linking the degree of lattice distortion to measured diffusion barriers and in isolating its effects from those of reactive element additions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of multiprincipal-element alloys with identical nominal compositions but differing in microstructure: one series processed (via rapid solidification or severe plastic deformation) to achieve a highly refined, high lattice distortion microstructure, and a control series processed under conventional conditions to yield coarser grains with lower lattice distortion. Subject both series to identical isothermal oxidation tests at 1200°C in ambient air for up to 500 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis of mass gain (oxidation kinetics)
Cross-sectional SEM/TEM imaging to assess oxide scale thickness, layering, and adherence
X-ray diffraction to identify oxide phases
Mechanical tests (e.g., adhesion or pull-off tests) to evaluate oxide scale robustness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with the refined, high lattice distortion microstructure do not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate constant, thinner and more adherent oxide scales, and superior mechanical integrity relative to the baseline coarse-grained alloys under identical test conditions, then the proposed mechanism—that a synergistic effect of lattice distortion (suppressing diffusion) and tailored microstructure (promoting layered oxide formation) governs oxidation resistance—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. ABSTRACTThe ongoing demand for high‐thrust turbine engines necessitates the advance of next‐generation structural materials capable of withstanding higher temperatures. Commercial MCrAlY alloy, used as bond coats crucial for thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems, face a fundamental temperature ceiling of ∼1100 °C due to accelerated oxidation and spallation. Here, we design a novel Y and Hf co‐doped NiCoCrAl‐type multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) that achieves exceptional 1200 °C oxidation resistance primarily through lattice distortion‐induced diffusion suppression. Compared with typical NiCoCrAlY alloy, the MPEA exhibits 59% lower in thermally grown oxide (TGO) growth rate, as well as negligible TGO spallation after 500 h at 1200°C. This performance stems from a significantly refined eutectic structure enabling rapid formation of a protective Al2O3 scale during initial oxidation, coupled with lattice distortion that elevates vacancy formation energy and Al migration barriers within the Al‐depletion zone (ADZ), drastically reducing sustained diffusion rates.
